# Two reproducible experiments

## Choose the model roles

The **direct Tweedie GLM is the tariff baseline**. A generalized linear model
(GLM) adds feature contributions on a chosen scale. Here its **log link** means
`log(expected rate) = intercept + feature contributions`: exponentiating gives
a positive rate, and coefficients become multiplicative tariff factors. Bins
and groups give the GLM discrete rating levels that we can inspect and export.

Tweedie with power 1.5 describes a non-negative cost outcome with both exact
zeros and positive continuous values. This suits a portfolio with many no-claim
policies and a few costly claims. We model the rate `claim_amount / exposure`,
using exposure as the weight; predictions are expected cost per policy-year.
The workflow derives that rate from the aggregate target column below.

The **raw-feature GBM is the flexible benchmark**. A gradient-boosted tree model
(GBM) adds trees sequentially to improve the fit. It can capture nonlinear
relationships and interactions without our explicit rating bins, but does not
directly give a simple multiplicative tariff. These roles are not a validated
model selection; we assess ranking and calibration in the next chapter.

{{< include _shared.qmd >}}

## Declare the data contract

`DatasetSpec.target` names aggregate policy claim cost, not a pre-divided rate.
The feature list deliberately excludes policy IDs, outcomes, exposure, and
review-only protected attributes. Special columns remain available to the
workflow for weighting and supervised preprocessing, without becoming predictors.

```{python}
from azoic.data import DatasetSpec
from azoic.workflow import ExperimentConfig, ModelSpec, PreprocessingSpec, run_experiment

portfolio = load_portfolio()
spec = DatasetSpec(
    target="claim_amount", exposure="exposure", claim_count="claim_count",
)
features = [
    "driver_age", "vehicle_age", "bonus_malus", "density", "region",
    "vehicle_brand", "veh_power", "veh_gas", "area",
]
```

`load_portfolio()` supplies this book's cleaned Parquet input. The standalone
[own-portfolio example](#use-your-own-portfolio) below replaces it with your file.

## Set training-only preprocessing

Tree bins pool numeric values; similarity groups pool categorical levels with
similar observed loss rates. The exposure and claim-count floors limit sparse
groups. All boundaries and memberships are learned **after splitting, on training
rows only**. Detailed merging rules and fitted memberships appear later.

```{python}
preprocessing = PreprocessingSpec(
    binner={
        "cols": ["driver_age", "vehicle_age", "bonus_malus", "density"],
        "strategy": "tree", "max_bins": 8, "min_exposure": 1000,
        "min_claims": 50, "random_state": 42,
    },
    grouper={
        "cols": ["region", "vehicle_brand", "veh_power", "veh_gas", "area"],
        "strategy": "similarity", "max_groups": 8, "min_exposure": 2000,
        "min_claims": 50,
    },
)
```

## Name the candidates

The GLM uses the log link and a small coefficient penalty (`alpha`) to temper
large fitted effects. Its Tweedie power stays at 1.5 throughout this comparison.

```{python}
direct_glm = ModelSpec(
    kind="glm",
    params={"family": "tweedie", "link": "log", "tweedie_power": 1.5, "alpha": 0.001},
)
```

The benchmark uses 100 trees with at most 31 leaves each; `learning_rate`
controls each tree's contribution. These are fixed tutorial settings, not a
claim that tuning has selected them.

```{python}
raw_gbm = ModelSpec(
    kind="gbm",
    params={
        "objective": "tweedie", "tweedie_variance_power": 1.5,
        "n_estimators": 100, "num_leaves": 31, "learning_rate": 0.05,
        "random_state": 42,
    },
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: the structured teacher

The third candidate is a GBM with the same tree settings, fitted after the
same kind of bins and groups as the GLM. Later, distillation fits a simple tariff
to this teacher's predictions. This extra candidate prepares that optional
lesson; understanding distillation is not required to fit the baseline.
The cell still executes when this explanation is collapsed.

```{python}
structured_teacher = raw_gbm.model_copy(deep=True)
```

:::

## Assemble and run the experiments

freMTPL2 has no suitable policy-time field. Both experiments therefore use the
same random seed and 20% holdout on the same ordered data. One experiment shares
preprocessing between its GLM and structured teacher; the other uses raw features.
The names identify these two runs and their three candidates in later chapters.

```{python}
glm_config = ExperimentConfig(
    name="fremtpl2-tariff-structured", data_path=str(PORTFOLIO_PATH),
    spec=spec, features=features, preprocessing=preprocessing,
    split="random", test_size=0.2, random_state=42,
    models={
        "direct-tweedie-glm": direct_glm,
        "tweedie-lightgbm-tariff": structured_teacher,
    },
)
gbm_config = ExperimentConfig(
    name="fremtpl2-raw-feature", data_path=str(PORTFOLIO_PATH),
    spec=spec.model_copy(), features=features,
    split="random", test_size=0.2, random_state=42,
    models={"tweedie-lightgbm": raw_gbm},
)
```

Other chapters use `make_experiment_configs` from `_shared.qmd` as the canonical
reusable configuration. This check prevents the visible version from drifting:

```{python}
assert (glm_config, gbm_config) == make_experiment_configs(str(PORTFOLIO_PATH))
```

Request fitted estimators explicitly so we can inspect and score with them.
The returned `Run` objects record metrics and the actual training/test positions.

```{python}
glm_run, glm_estimators = run_experiment(glm_config, return_estimators=True)
gbm_run, gbm_estimators = run_experiment(gbm_config, return_estimators=True)
runs = [glm_run, gbm_run]
estimators = {**glm_estimators, **gbm_estimators}
assert set(glm_run.models) == set(glm_config.models)
assert set(gbm_run.models) == set(gbm_config.models)
assert glm_run.data_fingerprint == gbm_run.data_fingerprint
assert glm_run.train_indices == gbm_run.train_indices
assert glm_run.test_indices == gbm_run.test_indices
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(portfolio, pd.read_parquet(PORTFOLIO_PATH))

train_idx = np.asarray(glm_run.train_indices, dtype=int)
test_idx = np.asarray(glm_run.test_indices, dtype=int)
assert len(train_idx) == glm_run.n_train
assert len(test_idx) == glm_run.n_test
assert np.intersect1d(train_idx, test_idx).size == 0
np.testing.assert_array_equal(
    np.sort(np.concatenate([train_idx, test_idx])), np.arange(len(portfolio))
)
```

The split happens before pipeline fitting, so the held-out outcomes cannot
influence the learned bins or groups. The returned positions identify the actual
random holdout; no second split is made. Positions refer to the exact input
frame in its original row order, not to index labels or policy IDs.

## Inspect the fitted tariff structure

Grouping relativities are `sum(claim_amount) / sum(exposure)`, and `min_claims`
is an aggregate claim-count floor. Nominal levels are stably sorted by risk;
ordered categories keep their declared order. Under-credible groups merge with
their closest-risk neighbour, then the closest adjacent pairs merge until the
group limit is met. Each merge recomputes aggregate risk, with distance ties
going left.

These are **training-fitted candidates for review**. Exposure and claim-count
floors do not establish statistical certainty. Tree cuts may change across
samples. Similarity grouping uses loss rates before adjustment for other
predictors, so membership is not an adjusted causal effect.

```{python}
train_frame = portfolio.iloc[train_idx].copy()
pd.testing.assert_index_equal(
    train_frame.index, portfolio.index.take(glm_run.train_indices)
)
y_train = train_frame["claim_amount"].to_numpy()
w_train = train_frame["exposure"].to_numpy()

raw_predict_columns = [*FEATURES, "exposure"]
special_predict_columns = [*FEATURES, "exposure", "claim_amount", "claim_count"]

glm_pipeline = glm_estimators["direct-tweedie-glm"]
fitted_preprocessing = glm_pipeline[:-1]
fitted_binner = glm_pipeline.named_steps["binner"]
fitted_grouper = glm_pipeline.named_steps["grouper"]
bin_snapshot = {name: edges.copy() for name, edges in fitted_binner.mapping_.items()}
group_snapshot = {name: mapping.copy() for name, mapping in fitted_grouper.mapping_.items()}
train_grouped = fitted_preprocessing.transform(train_frame[special_predict_columns])
train_grouped[["claim_count", "claim_amount"]] = train_frame[["claim_count", "claim_amount"]]

for feature in FEATURES:
    grouped = train_grouped.groupby(feature, observed=True, sort=True, dropna=False)
    summary = grouped.agg(
        policies=("exposure", "size"), exposure=("exposure", "sum"),
        claim_count=("claim_count", "sum"), claim_amount=("claim_amount", "sum"),
    )
    summary["observed_pure_premium"] = summary.claim_amount / summary.exposure
    if feature in fitted_grouper.mapping_:
        mapping = fitted_grouper.mapping_[feature]
        summary["members"] = [
            ", ".join(str(level) for level, group in mapping.items() if group == label)
            for label in summary.index
        ]
    assert summary.policies.sum() == len(train_frame)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(
        summary[["exposure", "claim_count", "claim_amount"]].sum(),
        train_frame[["exposure", "claim_count", "claim_amount"]].sum(),
    )
    display(summary.drop(columns="claim_amount").reset_index().rename(columns={
        "claim_count": "claims", "observed_pure_premium": "observed rate",
    }))
```

Intervals are lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive at finite boundaries. Within
each chapter, scoring and diagnostics reuse its training-fitted pipeline without
refitting mappings. Other chapters recreate the same experiment in their own kernel.

Continue to [essential diagnostics](03-diagnostics.qmd) to assess these candidates.

## Use your own portfolio

Start with one GLM and explicit columns. This standalone example needs Azoic,
pandas, and a Parquet file named `my_portfolio.parquet` in your working directory;
it does not use the book's loader or shared helpers. Each row is a policy period,
`paid_claims` is its non-negative aggregate cost, and `insured_years` is finite
exposure in years, at least one day (`1/366`, with 0.1% tolerance).
`driver_age` and `vehicle_age` are numeric.
Clean missing/invalid values and choose a consistent loss layer before fitting.

```python
import pandas as pd

from azoic.data import DatasetSpec
from azoic.workflow import ExperimentConfig, ModelSpec, run_experiment

my_features = ["driver_age", "vehicle_age"]
my_config = ExperimentConfig(
    name="my-first-tariff",
    data_path="my_portfolio.parquet",
    spec=DatasetSpec(target="paid_claims", exposure="insured_years"),
    features=my_features,
    split="random", test_size=0.2, random_state=42,
    models={
        "direct-glm": ModelSpec(
            kind="glm",
            params={"family": "tweedie", "link": "log", "tweedie_power": 1.5,
                    "alpha": 0.001},
        ),
    },
)
my_run, my_estimators = run_experiment(my_config, return_estimators=True)
my_portfolio = pd.read_parquet(my_config.data_path)
scoring_rows = my_portfolio.iloc[list(my_run.test_indices)][[*my_features, "insured_years"]]
scored = scoring_rows.copy()
scored["raw_rate"] = my_estimators["direct-glm"].predict(scoring_rows)
scored["expected_period_cost"] = scored["raw_rate"] * scored["insured_years"]
print(scored.head())
```

The scoring frame contains no claim outcomes. These are raw model rates: no
training O/P adjustment has been applied. The simple GLM here uses numeric ages
directly, so log rate is linear in each age; add the preprocessing shown above
when discrete rating levels are needed. Do not copy freMTPL2 credibility floors
without considering your portfolio's exposure and claims volume.

Keep identifiers, outcomes, and protected attributes out of `features`; name any
review-only protected columns in `DatasetSpec.protected_cols`. Exposure is a
weight, carried into prediction as shown, not a rating feature. Keep the source
row order unchanged when using the returned positions.

Python relative paths use the process working directory. With
`ExperimentConfig.from_yaml`, relative data paths instead resolve from the YAML
file's directory; see the [experiment guide](https://thomasbury.github.io/azoic/guide/experiment-configuration/).
Use a random split when no real time field exists. If deployment means pricing
future periods, use a genuine policy-time column and the
[temporal recipe](08-temporal-stability.qmd); never invent time from row order.
Choose revisions inside training data and reserve fresh evaluation data once
you have used the displayed holdout to make decisions.

## Optional: pool sparse risks and limit model flexibility {#regularization-controls}

Sparse ages or vehicle categories can show large changes in predicted pure
premium because a small amount of data has too much influence. Use the existing
`PreprocessingSpec` and `ModelSpec.params` settings to compare a few deliberate
alternatives:

| Action in Azoic | What it can achieve | What it does not guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Increase `AutoBinner.min_exposure` or `min_claims`, or reduce `max_bins`. | Merge neighbouring age intervals so sparse tails share information with a larger group. | Smooth transitions between bins, or enough evidence for every combination of rating factors. |
| Use the learned bins for a GBM as well as a GLM. | Prevent age distinctions inside a bin, holding other inputs fixed. | The best possible GBM: pooling can hide real differences, and other features can still split a bin into sparse leaves. |
| Increase `AutoGrouper.min_exposure` or `min_claims`, or reduce `max_groups`. | Pool sparse categorical levels, such as vehicle brands, using the configured grouping strategy. | Similar risk after accounting for other features: similarity grouping uses unadjusted loss rates. |
| Increase `RiskGLM.alpha`, keeping `l1_ratio=0` for an L2 penalty. | Pull fitted coefficients towards zero and temper extreme effects. | Similar factors for adjacent ages: the penalty does not connect neighbouring bins. |
| Reduce `RiskGBM.num_leaves`, set a smaller positive `max_depth`, increase `min_child_samples`, or increase `reg_lambda`. | Limit detailed interactions or shrink leaf estimates, making isolated fluctuations harder to fit. | A minimum exposure per leaf: `min_child_samples` controls observation support, not an exposure floor. |

If ages 80–95 share one bin, the model cannot use that age feature to charge an
otherwise identical 93-year-old differently from an 82-year-old. Bins create
flat steps with possible boundary jumps, not continuous curves. LightGBM's
internal histogram bins do not replace Azoic's exposure and claim-count floors.

Use a direction constraint only when the risk relationship supports it.
`RiskGBM.monotone_constraints` can require a numeric feature's predicted effect
to increase or decrease, holding other inputs fixed. Azoic rejects nonzero
constraints on categorical features, including `AutoBinner` interval categories.
Driver age need not have one direction across the whole age range.
`AutoBinner.monotonic` influences how training bins are merged; it does **not**
constrain the premiums subsequently fitted by the GLM or GBM.

## Check that stability has improved

Compare the raw-feature GBM, the binned GBM, and the simpler tariff on the same
validation rows. Review exposure-weighted Tweedie deviance, portfolio and
segment O/P, and age profiles. Refit on repeated training samples to see whether
tail premiums and learned boundaries move substantially. Relearn supervised bins
and groups within each training fold, and choose settings using validation
inside the outer training data. Keep the final test set for one evaluation.

Prefer the simpler candidate when predictive performance is comparable and
tail premiums are materially more stable. The evidence comes from these
comparisons, not from a smooth line or an exposure threshold alone.
